title: Changing trends and career in physical education
subject: Physical Education
summary: Physical education uses movement and sport to develop the whole person, and it now offers a wide range of careers.
points: The scope covers health, fitness, recreation, rehabilitation and competitive sport.
Careers include teaching, coaching, sports journalism, sports medicine, physiotherapy, sports management and fitness training.
Ancient and modern traditions both shaped physical education, from yoga and akharas to Olympic sport.
Competitions are organised at school, district, state, national and international levels.
example: A student who enjoys sport can train as a coach, a physiotherapist or a sports manager without becoming a professional athlete.
mistakes: Treating physical education as only games — it also covers health, first aid, yoga and recreation.
Assuming it is not an academic subject — it has a full board syllabus and theory paper.
aliases: changing trends and career in physical education

title: Olympism and the Olympic movement
subject: Physical Education
summary: The Olympic movement promotes sport with friendship, respect and fair play, and India has its own Olympic and Paralympic history.
points: The ancient games were held at Olympia; the modern games were revived by Pierre de Coubertin in 1896.
The Olympic values are excellence, friendship and respect, expressed in the motto Faster, Higher, Stronger — Together.
The Olympic symbols include the five rings, the flame, the flag and the oath.
India has won Olympic medals mainly in hockey, shooting, wrestling, badminton, boxing and athletics.
example: The five interlocking rings stand for the union of the five continents and athletes meeting in fair competition.
mistakes: Confusing the Olympic motto with the Olympic oath.
Believing the modern Olympics began in ancient Greece — the modern series started in 1896 in Athens.

title: Yoga and lifestyle
subject: Physical Education
summary: Yoga combines postures, breathing and meditation to improve physical and mental health and to prevent lifestyle diseases.
points: Ashtanga yoga has eight limbs, from yama and niyama through asana and pranayama to dhyana and samadhi.
Common asanas include tadasana, vajrasana, bhujangasana, shavasana and trikonasana.
Pranayama such as anulom-vilom and kapalbhati works on breath control.
Yoga helps obesity, diabetes, asthma, hypertension and stress when practised regularly.
example: Bhujangasana (cobra pose) strengthens the spine and opens the chest, and is often suggested for mild back stiffness.
mistakes: Practising advanced asanas without warm-up or guidance.
Thinking yoga only means physical postures — the eight limbs include ethical and mental practice.

title: Physical education and sports for children with special needs
subject: Physical Education
summary: Adapted physical education gives children with disabilities equal access to movement, sport and recreation.
points: Disabilities may be physical, intellectual, visual, hearing or multiple.
Adapted programmes change equipment, rules, space and pace rather than excluding the child.
The Paralympics, Special Olympics and Deaflympics provide competitive pathways.
Inclusive teaching uses buddy support, modified equipment and clear demonstration.
example: A seated volleyball game with a lower net lets a student using a wheelchair take part on equal terms.
mistakes: Lowering expectations instead of adapting the activity.
Confusing the Paralympics (physical impairment) with the Special Olympics (intellectual disability).

title: Physical fitness, wellness and lifestyle
subject: Physical Education
summary: Physical fitness is the ability to carry out daily tasks without undue fatigue, and wellness adds mental and social health.
points: Health-related components are cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition.
Skill-related components are speed, agility, balance, coordination, power and reaction time.
Exercise, balanced diet, sleep and stress control build wellness.
Lifestyle diseases such as obesity, diabetes and hypertension are largely preventable.
example: A student of 50 kg and 1.6 m height has a BMI of about 19.5, inside the healthy range.
mistakes: Using centimetres instead of metres in the BMI formula.
Equating thinness with fitness.

title: Test, measurement and evaluation in sports
subject: Physical Education
summary: Tests measure fitness and skill so that training can be judged and improved.
points: Measurement gives a number; evaluation judges that number against a standard.
Common fitness tests include the 50 m dash, sit-ups, sit-and-reach, shuttle run and 600 m or 12-minute run.
The Harvard step test estimates cardiovascular endurance from recovery heart rate.
Test selection depends on validity, reliability, objectivity and the group being tested.

formulas.name: Harvard step test score
formulas.expr: fitness index = (duration of exercise in seconds × 100) ÷ (2 × sum of three recovery pulse counts)

example: A 12-minute run measures cardiovascular endurance; a sit-and-reach box measures flexibility.
mistakes: Using one test for every fitness component.
Ignoring standardised procedure, which destroys reliability.

title: Fundamentals of anatomy, physiology and kinesiology in sports
subject: Physical Education
summary: Anatomy describes the body's structure, physiology its functions, and kinesiology the mechanics of movement.
points: The skeletal system gives support, protection and leverage; the adult skeleton has 206 bones.
Muscles produce movement by contraction, working in opposing pairs.
The circulatory and respiratory systems supply oxygen and remove waste during exercise.
Kinesiology studies movement in terms of axes, planes and joint action.
example: Bending the elbow is flexion, produced by the biceps contracting while the triceps relaxes.
mistakes: Saying muscles push — they can only pull.
Mixing the sagittal plane with the frontal plane.

title: Biomechanics in sports
subject: Physical Education
summary: Biomechanics applies the laws of mechanics to human movement to improve technique and reduce injury.
points: Newton's three laws explain force, acceleration and reaction in sport.
Levers in the body are first, second and third class, with most joints acting as third-class levers.
Projectile motion depends on angle, speed and height of release.
Balance depends on the base of support and the centre of gravity.

formulas.name: Optimum projection angle
formulas.expr: about 45° for maximum range without air resistance

example: A long jumper raises the centre of gravity at take-off and lands with the feet forward to gain distance.
mistakes: Thinking a larger angle always gives a longer throw — past about 45° range falls again.
Confusing mass with weight.

title: Psychology and sports
subject: Physical Education
summary: Sport psychology studies how personality, motivation, anxiety and aggression affect performance.
points: Personality is described by trait and type approaches and by the big five factors.
Motivation is intrinsic or extrinsic, and drive theory links arousal to performance.
Anxiety can be cognitive or somatic; the inverted-U principle says moderate arousal helps performance.
Aggression may be hostile or instrumental, and can be channelled into assertive play.
example: A cricketer who practises for the love of the game shows intrinsic motivation; one playing only for prize money is extrinsically motivated.
mistakes: Believing the highest arousal always gives the best performance.
Treating assertion (fair, forceful play) as aggression.

title: Training in sports
subject: Physical Education
summary: Training is planned, repeated exercise that improves fitness and skill while allowing recovery.
points: Strength, endurance, speed and flexibility each need their own training method.
A training session has a warm-up, the conditioning part and a cool-down.
The principles of training include overload, progression, specificity, reversibility and recovery.
Periodisation divides the year into preparatory, competition and transition phases.
example: A 16-year-old training at 70 per cent of maximum has a target heart rate of about 143 beats per minute.
mistakes: Increasing load too fast, which causes injury instead of progress.
Skipping rest days — adaptation happens during recovery.

title: Doping in sports
subject: Physical Education
summary: Doping is the use of banned performance-enhancing substances or methods, and it is prohibited in sport.
points: Banned classes include stimulants, anabolic steroids, peptide hormones, diuretics and narcotics.
Blood doping and gene doping are prohibited methods.
Doping harms health: liver damage, hormonal imbalance, heart problems and dependence.
WADA sets the code, and NADA enforces testing in India.
example: An anabolic steroid may build muscle but can damage the liver and shut down natural hormone production.
mistakes: Assuming only 'hard' drugs count — diuretics used to mask other substances are also banned.
Believing supplements are always safe — some contain prohibited substances.

title: Planning in sports
subject: Physical Education
summary: Planning organises tournaments and training so that time, money and facilities are used efficiently.
points: Tournaments may be knockout, league, combination or challenge formats.
A knockout needs the number of matches to be counted in advance; a league gives every team a chance.
Fixtures for a league are drawn by the cyclic method; byes are given in knockouts when entries are not a power of two.
A good plan sets objectives, assigns duties, and prepares budget, schedule and equipment.

formulas.name: Byes
formulas.expr: byes = next power of two − number of teams

example: With 11 teams, a knockout needs 10 matches, and the next power of two is 16, so 5 byes are given.
mistakes: Using the league formula for a knockout.
Ignoring byes, which leaves an uneven bracket.

title: Sports and nutrition
subject: Physical Education
summary: Athletes need a balanced diet matched to training load, with carbohydrate for fuel and protein for repair.
points: Macronutrients are carbohydrates, proteins and fats; micronutrients are vitamins and minerals.
Carbohydrate loading raises glycogen stores before endurance events.
Protein needs rise with strength training; excess protein is not stored as muscle.
Hydration and electrolytes matter, and eating should be timed around training.
example: A runner eats a carbohydrate-rich meal three hours before a race and drinks water at intervals during it.
mistakes: Believing more protein alone builds muscle.
Cutting salt and water completely before competition.

title: Children and women in sports
subject: Physical Education
summary: Motor development, exercise safety and equal opportunity shape sport for children and for women.
points: Motor development proceeds from gross to fine movement and follows a predictable sequence.
Children need age-appropriate load, varied activity and protection from overtraining.
Girls face unequal access, fewer facilities and social expectations in sport.
Menarche, bone health and iron status need attention in female athletes.
example: A primary child should build coordination through games rather than heavy strength training.
mistakes: Applying adult training loads to growing children.
Using the female athlete triad — low energy, menstrual disruption, low bone density — as a training goal.

title: Physiology and injuries in sports
subject: Physical Education
summary: Exercise changes the heart, lungs and muscles, and injuries need prompt first aid and graded return.
points: Cardiac output rises during exercise through higher heart rate and stroke volume.
Training enlarges stroke volume and improves oxygen uptake.
Soft-tissue injuries include sprain, strain and contusion; hard-tissue injuries include fracture and dislocation.
First aid follows rest, ice, compression and elevation, with medical help for serious injury.

formulas.name: Cardiac output
formulas.expr: cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume

example: A twisted ankle is a sprain: ice and compression for the first 24 to 48 hours reduce swelling.
mistakes: Applying heat immediately to a fresh sprain.
Returning to play before a fracture has healed.

title: Elements and principles of visual art
subject: Fine Arts
summary: Visual art is built from elements such as line, colour and form, organised by principles such as balance and rhythm.
points: The elements are line, shape, form, space, texture, value and colour.
The principles are balance, rhythm, emphasis, proportion, unity, contrast and movement.
Colour theory covers primary, secondary and tertiary colours, and warm and cool families.
Composition decides where the eye goes first and how the parts hold together.
example: A painting that repeats a curve in the drapery and the hills uses rhythm to hold the composition together.
mistakes: Mixing the elements (line, colour) with the principles (balance, rhythm).
Using many strong colours without a focal point.

title: Indian art: prehistoric to early Buddhist art
subject: Fine Arts
summary: Indian art begins with rock paintings and Indus seals, and matures in Buddhist stupas, sculpture and cave painting.
points: Bhimbetka rock shelters show prehistoric hunting and dancing scenes.
Indus artefacts include the bronze dancing girl and steatite seals.
The Great Stupa at Sanchi has a hemispherical dome, gateways and carved railings.
Ajanta cave paintings depict Jataka stories with a strong sense of volume and gesture.
example: The Sanchi gateway carvings show the Buddha through symbols such as footprints, a wheel and a tree rather than a human figure.
mistakes: Calling every ancient Indian image of the Buddha anthropomorphic — early art used symbols.
Mixing Ajanta (Buddhist caves) with Ellora (Hindu, Buddhist and Jain caves).

title: Indian art: temple, Mughal, Rajput and modern
subject: Fine Arts
summary: Indian art moves from temple sculpture and Mughal miniature painting to Rajput schools and the modern Indian artists.
points: Nagara and Dravida temple styles differ in shikhara and gateway forms.
Mughal painting began with Akbar's illustrated manuscripts and peaked in Jahangir's naturalism.
Rajasthani and Pahari schools are known for Krishna themes, flat colour and lyrical composition.
The Bengal School and artists such as Amrita Sher-Gil and Jamini Roy shaped modern Indian art.
example: A Pahari miniature often places Krishna and Radha in a lush landscape, using colour to carry the mood.
mistakes: Treating Mughal and Rajput painting as the same school.
Assuming modern Indian art began only after independence.

title: Western art: Renaissance to modern
subject: Fine Arts
summary: Western art moved from religious medieval imagery through Renaissance realism to modern abstraction.
points: The Renaissance introduced perspective, anatomy and humanist subject matter.
Baroque art used dramatic light; impressionism turned to light and momentary effect.
Cubism broke form into facets, and expressionism used colour for feeling.
Each movement answered the technology and politics of its time, including photography.
example: Impressionist painters worked outdoors to catch changing light, which became possible with portable paint tubes.
mistakes: Calling all pre-modern Western art Renaissance.
Assuming abstraction means no skill — it is a deliberate choice about form.

title: Home Science: concept and scope
subject: Home Science
summary: Home Science applies science to everyday life in food, clothing, shelter, resource use and human development.
points: Its fields are human development, food and nutrition, fabric and apparel, resource management and housing.
It is interdisciplinary, drawing on biology, chemistry, economics, sociology and psychology.
Careers include dietetics, textile design, interior design, early childhood education and consumer services.
The subject emphasises practical problem solving for families and communities.
example: A Home Science student may plan a low-cost balanced diet for a family, which combines nutrition and resource management.
mistakes: Treating Home Science as cooking only — it spans five distinct fields.
Ignoring the science behind the practice, such as nutrient loss in cooking.

title: Human development across the life span
subject: Home Science
summary: Development runs from infancy to old age through physical, cognitive, social and emotional change.
points: Development is lifelong, multidimensional and influenced by heredity and environment.
Infancy and early childhood focus on attachment, motor skills and language.
Adolescence brings puberty, identity formation and peer influence.
Adulthood and old age bring career, family, health and adjustment tasks.
example: A toddler learning to walk shows gross motor development before fine motor control such as holding a crayon.
mistakes: Treating development as only physical growth.
Assuming all children reach milestones at exactly the same age.

title: Food, nutrition and health
subject: Home Science
summary: Nutrition studies how nutrients in food support growth, health and protection from disease.
points: Nutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and fibre.
Deficiency diseases include anaemia from iron lack and goitre from iodine lack.
Food safety covers hygiene, storage, adulteration and preservation.
Meal planning balances nutrients, cost, season and family needs.
example: Adding lemon to a dal salad helps iron absorption because vitamin C aids it.
mistakes: Assuming a costly diet is automatically nutritious.
Overcooking vegetables, which destroys water-soluble vitamins.

title: Fabric and apparel
subject: Home Science
summary: Fibre becomes yarn, yarn becomes fabric, and fabric becomes clothing chosen for climate, use and care.
points: Fibres are natural (cotton, silk, wool) or man-made (rayon, polyester, nylon).
Yarn is made by spinning, and fabric by weaving, knitting or non-woven methods.
Fabric finishes such as mercerising, waterproofing and wrinkle resistance change performance.
Clothing choice considers fibre properties, care, cost and the wearer's needs.
example: Cotton absorbs sweat well, which is why it suits summer clothing, while polyester dries faster.
mistakes: Calling rayon natural — it is regenerated from cellulose.
Ignoring care labels, which leads to shrinkage or colour loss.

title: Resource management and housing
subject: Home Science
summary: Resource management uses time, money, energy and skills efficiently, and housing provides a safe, functional space.
points: Resources are human (time, energy, skills) and non-human (money, material, facilities).
Management steps are planning, organising, controlling and evaluating.
Work simplification saves time and energy through better layout and equipment.
Housing needs light, ventilation, safety, privacy and space for activities.
example: Keeping frequently used utensils near the cooking area is work simplification by layout.
mistakes: Treating money as the only resource.
Planning a household budget without an emergency margin.

title: Entrepreneurship: concept and functions
subject: Entrepreneurship
summary: An entrepreneur spots an opportunity, takes risk and organises resources to create value.
points: Entrepreneurship is the process of setting up and running an enterprise while bearing risk.
Functions include idea generation, resource mobilisation, management and risk bearing.
An entrepreneur differs from a manager (employee) and from an intrapreneur (inside a firm).
Entrepreneurship drives innovation, employment and regional development.
example: A student who starts a small tutoring service, rents a room and hires two tutors is performing the entrepreneurial functions.
mistakes: Confusing an entrepreneur with an investor who only supplies money.
Assuming entrepreneurship needs a large initial investment.

title: Entrepreneurial journey and competencies
subject: Entrepreneurship
summary: The entrepreneurial journey moves from idea to start-up to growth, and depends on specific competencies.
points: The journey has idea generation, feasibility study, business plan, launch and growth.
Competencies include initiative, self-confidence, problem solving, perseverance and information seeking.
Ethics and social responsibility shape whether a venture lasts.
Failure is treated as learning, and pivoting is a normal part of the journey.
example: A venture that starts as a home bakery may pivot to supplying cafés once demand is understood.
mistakes: Skipping the feasibility check and launching on enthusiasm alone.
Treating one failed attempt as the end of the entrepreneurial career.

title: Understanding the market
subject: Entrepreneurship
summary: Understanding the market means knowing customers, competitors, price and the way value is delivered.
points: Market research gathers primary and secondary information about demand.
Segmentation groups customers by need, age, income or location.
The marketing mix has product, price, place and promotion.
Competitor analysis shows where a venture can differentiate.
example: A tiffin service segments students by hostel location and prices a weekly plan to suit them.
mistakes: Assuming everyone is a customer.
Pricing by copying a competitor without checking costs.

title: Business finance and arithmetic
subject: Entrepreneurship
summary: Ventures need capital for fixed and working needs, and break-even analysis shows when costs are recovered.
points: Funds are raised through own capital, loans, angel investors or venture capital.
Fixed capital buys assets; working capital runs day-to-day operations.
Break-even point is where total revenue equals total cost.
Cash flow and margin matter more than turnover alone for survival.

formulas.name: Break-even quantity
formulas.expr: BEP = fixed cost ÷ (selling price − variable cost per unit)

formulas.name: Break-even sales
formulas.expr: BEP sales = fixed cost ÷ contribution ratio

example: Fixed cost ₹10,000, price ₹50 and variable cost ₹30 give a break-even of 500 units.
mistakes: Using profit instead of contribution in the break-even formula.
Forgetting working capital when planning the launch.

title: Entrepreneurial planning, marketing and growth
subject: Entrepreneurship
summary: A business plan turns an idea into a funded, launched and growing venture.
points: A business plan covers the idea, market, operations, organisation, finance and risk.
Marketing for a start-up uses low-cost promotion, referrals and digital channels.
Growth strategies include franchising, licensing, mergers and diversification.
Resource mobilisation covers finance, people, technology and networks.
example: A small café grows by franchising its format rather than opening every outlet itself.
mistakes: Writing a plan with no realistic cash-flow projection.
Growing faster than working capital allows.

title: Indian legal system and sources of law
subject: Legal Studies
summary: Indian law comes from the Constitution, legislation, precedents, customs and personal laws.
points: The Constitution is the supreme law, and all other law must conform to it.
Legislation is made by Parliament and state legislatures.
Precedent means following earlier judgments of higher courts.
Customs and personal laws govern marriage, inheritance and religious practice.
example: A High Court judgment binds lower courts in its state, which is the doctrine of precedent.
mistakes: Treating a statute and a judgment as the same kind of source.
Assuming customary law has no legal standing.

title: Courts and the judiciary
subject: Legal Studies
summary: The judiciary interprets law through a hierarchy from the Supreme Court down to district and subordinate courts.
points: The Supreme Court is the apex court, followed by High Courts and district courts.
Jurisdiction may be original, appellate or advisory.
Judicial review lets courts strike down law that violates the Constitution.
Independence of the judiciary is protected by tenure, salary and appointment safeguards.
example: A writ petition for a fundamental right can go directly to a High Court or the Supreme Court.
mistakes: Thinking a district court can overrule a High Court.
Confusing appellate jurisdiction with original jurisdiction.

title: Law of contract and law of torts
subject: Legal Studies
summary: Contract law enforces agreements, while tort law compensates for civil wrongs outside contract.
points: A valid contract needs offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity, free consent and lawful object.
A contract without consideration is generally void, apart from exceptions.
Torts include negligence, defamation, nuisance and trespass.
Remedies in tort are mainly damages and injunction.
example: A cyclist who injures a pedestrian by careless riding commits the tort of negligence and may have to pay damages.
mistakes: Calling every broken promise a tort — a breach of contract is not a tort.
Ignoring free consent, which makes an agreement voidable.

title: Criminal justice and family justice
subject: Legal Studies
summary: Criminal law punishes offences against society, while family law deals with marriage, divorce, maintenance and custody.
points: A crime has actus reus and mens rea, and the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
The criminal process runs from FIR to investigation, trial and appeal.
Family disputes are handled by family courts, with mediation often preferred.
Personal laws differ by religion, and the Special Marriage Act allows civil marriage.
example: Theft requires both the act of taking and the intention to take dishonestly.
mistakes: Applying the criminal standard of proof to a civil suit.
Assuming one personal law applies to every citizen.

title: Human rights, ADR and the legal profession
subject: Legal Studies
summary: Human rights protect basic freedoms, alternative dispute resolution avoids full trials, and lawyers serve both clients and the court.
points: Human rights are protected by the Constitution and by international instruments such as the UDHR.
ADR includes arbitration, mediation, conciliation and lok adalat.
ADR is faster and cheaper but may not suit cases needing enforcement or precedent.
Advocates have duties to the client, the court and the profession, set by the Bar Council.
example: A consumer dispute settled in a lok adalat avoids years of litigation and court fees.
mistakes: Thinking ADR awards never need enforcement.
Believing a lawyer's only duty is to win, ignoring duties to the court.

title: Informatics Practices: Python and data handling
subject: Informatics Practices
summary: Informatics Practices uses Python to handle data, from basic types and control flow to lists and dictionaries.
points: Python data types include int, float, str, bool, list, tuple and dict.
Control flow uses if, for and while, with break and continue.
Lists are mutable and indexed from zero; dictionaries store key-value pairs.
Good practice means readable names, comments and testing small pieces.
example: A dictionary of student marks allows lookup by name without scanning a list.
mistakes: Expecting a tuple to change after creation — tuples are immutable.
Confusing = (assignment) with == (comparison).

title: Data handling with pandas and visualisation
subject: Informatics Practices
summary: pandas organises data into Series and DataFrames, and plotting turns it into readable charts.
points: A Series is one-dimensional; a DataFrame is a table of columns.
Data can be read from CSV, cleaned, filtered and grouped.
Missing values are handled by dropping or filling them.
Matplotlib plots include line, bar, histogram and scatter charts.
example: Grouping a marks DataFrame by section gives the average score per section in one line.
mistakes: Forgetting that DataFrame indexing includes column names as well as rows.
Plotting without labels or a title, which makes the chart unreadable.

title: SQL, computer networks and societal impacts
subject: Informatics Practices
summary: Databases answer questions with SQL, networks connect systems, and both carry social and ethical consequences.
points: SQL commands include SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY and aggregate functions.
Keys link tables: primary key, foreign key and candidate key.
Networks are described by topology and by device, such as LAN, WAN, switch and router.
Societal concerns include privacy, cyber crime, digital divide and e-waste.
example: SELECT section, AVG(marks) FROM students GROUP BY section gives one average per section.
mistakes: Using WHERE where HAVING is needed after grouping.
Assuming a foreign key must be unique — it may repeat.
